The purpose is to gain fetal maturity while closely monitoring for complications.
This is an important PPROM distinction.
Unlike uncomplicated preterm labour with intact membranes, **PPROM generally requires antibiotic therapy to reduce infection and prolong latency**, according to guideline and local protocol.
NICE recommends offering erythromycin to women with PPROM and advises against co-amoxiclav for prophylaxis. (nice.org.uk)

subsections.subsection_title: 48. EXPLAIN WHY THE BABY MAY NEED NICU

blocks.title: Depending on gestation, the baby may require:

blocks.text: **"The membranes around your baby appear to have ruptured earlier than expected. At this stage of pregnancy, the main concerns are infection and premature birth. We will monitor you closely for signs of infection, monitor your baby's wellbeing and involve the neonatal team. Depending on your gestational age and how you and the baby are doing, we may be able to continue the pregnancy safely for some time. If infection, significant bleeding, fetal compromise or another complication develops, delivery may become necessary."**

**"This is a 29-year-old G2P1 at 31+4 weeks presenting with a sudden gush of clear fluid followed by continued leakage. She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable, with no uterine tenderness or vaginal bleeding. The fetal heart rate is reassuring and there are no significant contractions. Sterile speculum examination demonstrates clear fluid pooling in the posterior fornix, consistent with rupture of membranes. There are currently no clinical features of intrauterine infection or fetal compromise. I would manage this as PPROM with appropriate antibiotics, antenatal corticosteroids and close maternal and fetal monitoring, with neonatal involvement."**

**"This is a 30-year-old woman at 29 weeks with confirmed PPROM who is now febrile at 38.7°C, tachycardic and has uterine tenderness. The fetal heart rate is 175 bpm and the liquor is offensive. These findings are highly concerning for intrauterine infection/chorioamnionitis. I would initiate maternal sepsis management, commence appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotics, involve the senior obstetric and neonatal teams and plan delivery after maternal stabilisation rather than continuing expectant management."**

**"This is a 28-year-old at 30 weeks with confirmed PPROM. She is currently haemodynamically stable and afebrile, but the CTG demonstrates persistent fetal bradycardia with recurrent decelerations. This represents fetal compromise requiring urgent senior obstetric review and preparation for expedited delivery. Tocolysis would not be appropriate."**

**"This woman with PPROM has developed acute fetal bradycardia, and the umbilical cord is palpable in the vagina. This is cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency. I would call for immediate assistance, relieve cord compression by elevating the presenting part and positioning the mother appropriately, and arrange urgent delivery, usually by Caesarean section if vaginal birth is not immediately achievable."**

**"This is a 31-week pregnant woman with confirmed PPROM who has subsequently developed regular painful contractions with progressive cervical dilatation. She is currently afebrile and haemodynamically stable and the fetal heart rate is reassuring. This represents PPROM complicated by established preterm labour. I would involve the neonatal and senior obstetric teams, administer antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate where indicated, assess whether there is any evidence of infection or fetal compromise and plan delivery according to the clinical circumstances."**
**Rupture of the fetal membranes before 37 weeks and before the onset of labour.**

blocks.text:
**W — When did the fluid leak?**
**A — Assess mother and fetus**
**T — Temperature/infection**
**E — Examine with sterile speculum**
**R — Rupture confirmed? Gestational age?**
**S — Steroids, antibiotics, surveillance and specialist/neonatal planning**
**"Is there a reason she needs delivery now?"**
That single question prevents a major OSCE mistake.

**"I would first assess maternal and fetal wellbeing and confirm the gestational age. I would take a focused history regarding the onset, amount, colour and odour of the fluid, contractions, vaginal bleeding, fetal movements and symptoms of infection. I would check maternal observations, particularly temperature and pulse, perform an abdominal examination assessing uterine tenderness, contractions and fetal presentation, and assess the fetal heart rate.**

**I would perform a sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid, bleeding, cervical dilatation and evidence of infection, while avoiding unnecessary digital vaginal examination. I would investigate with appropriate maternal blood tests, urine testing, cultures where indicated, CTG and ultrasound.**

**If PPROM is confirmed and mother and fetus are stable without infection or another indication for delivery, I would involve the senior obstetric and neonatal teams and manage expectantly according to gestational age and local protocol. This would include latency antibiotics, antenatal corticosteroids when indicated, consideration of magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection at very preterm gestations, and close maternal and fetal surveillance.**

**If there is chorioamnionitis, significant abruption, fetal compromise, cord prolapse, maternal deterioration or another indication for delivery, I would initiate appropriate emergency management and arrange delivery after maternal stabilisation."**
**PPROM → GESTATION → MOTHER → FETUS → SPECULUM → INFECTION → BLEEDING → CONTRACTIONS → STEROIDS → ANTIBIOTICS → MgSO₄ → NEONATAL TEAM → EXPECTANT vs DELIVERY**
**PPROM does NOT automatically mean immediate delivery.**
If mother and fetus are stable and there is no contraindication to continuing pregnancy → **expectant management may be appropriate.**
If infection, major bleeding or fetal/maternal compromise develops → **delivery becomes necessary.**
